entries.note: Descriptions of mechanism of English credit institutions, with able discussions of many points of theory.
Shows that tendency to substitute credit in place of material substances is the distinctive mark of progress in the art of effecting exchange.

Contents: Three centuries of cheap money in the United States; Paper currency of North Carolina: Paper currency of New Hampshire. Bibliography, p. 275-88. General thesis: Inflationist movement always due to scarcity of capital in sparsely settled regions.
entries.noteSource: D. R. Dewey in Amer. hist. r. 6: 579.

entries.note: Bibliography by Hugh Williams, p. 347-77. Defines terms, discusses indications, accompanying conditions, causes and preventives; brief history of crises and depressions in United States. Diagrams, index.
What funds are, how obtained and how operated through U. S. treasury, savings and commercial banks, building associations, brokerage, trust and insurance companies. Facsimiles of business paper.
List of authorities, p. 577-81.
Mainly a balancing of arguments. No one book will give an intelligent reader a better grasp of the controversy.
Succinct account of fundamental character of banking operations, nature of credit and its practical manifestation in the chief forms, checks and banknotes.
Partial list of authorities, p. 429-32. No one else has been so successful in obtaining useful information on this subject within the limits proposed.

Bibliography, p. 435-99. 1776-1860, coinage system, paper currency; 1861-90, U.S. legal tender notes, silver question, national banking system; 1891-1902, silver contest of 1896, reform act of 1900. General review, bibliography. U. S. laws and other documents in appendix.
Elementary. Contains descriptions of clearinghouse and check bank. Excellent for laying a basis of sound doctrines.
Special emphasis on constitutionality of government paper money. Historical rather than controversial; not exhaustive, but adequate.
By a monometalist. Serviceable historical compendium, if reader bears in mind that author writes to persuade.
Bibliographies. Comprehensive treatment. First of a proposed series of 6 volumes on money and banking.
List of references, p. 353-63. Intended for college use and as handbook for average citizen. On points at issue all important views are set forth clearly. Bibliographic references.
entries.noteSource: H. A. Mills in Annals Amer. acad. pol. sci. 22: 126.

entries.note: Reviews legislation and conditions from 1878 to close of 1896; advocates monometalism but considers bimetalist arguments fairly.
Reviews briefly history of gold and silver currency and argues strongly for international bimetalism. Opposes free coinage of silver.
States and impartially examines various theories. Holds that paper money nominally or really convertible into eoin is liable to overissue.
First published in 1879. An abridgment of Money, with added chapters.
History of gold and silver coinage in U.S. beginning with Massachusetts colonial mint, 1652. Opposes free coinage of silver.
Bibliographies. Treats evolution of money, the gold standard, fiat money as developed in colonial, continental and federal curreney, and banks,
Bibliography about registration, p. 26-28. Explains systems in various countries.
Reviews the doctrines of Carey, Bastiat, Mill, Leroy- Beaulien and George as to rent. From conservative standpoint.
For charity workers and working men seeking good methods of saving.
A sketch of conditions before and during time of Robert Owen; a history of subsequent experiments, with sugges tions.
The carlier essays appeared under title The religion of socialism.
Biographie notes on socialist writers and leaders, p. 205-63; bibliography, p. 234-86.
Impartial presentation, brief and clear.
Bibliography, p. 399-112. Examines its nature, strength and weakness; concedes merits generously but in the main disapproves, though advocating socialization of monopolies.
Contents: Utopian socialism; Materialist conception of history; Scientifle socialism; Apx. The mark.
The 86 tracts are bound in order of number. Those missing are out of print or withdrawn. The great propaganda of English socialism.
Endeavors to show that principal cause of poverty and wretchedness in midst of wealth and abundance is private ownership of land. Style engaging and often eloquent. Basis of single tax" theory.
Select bibliography, p. 367-70. Maintains that socialism and extreme forms of individualism are alike unamerican, and that moral improvement is more needed than economie changes.
Historical and critical, with examination of proposed remedies for low wages and unemployed labor, and of eight-hour working day.
Statement of case for state socialism, with plans for its operation.
Limited to 19th century. Gives friendly interpretation to theories: opposes state control and advocates a socialism only equivalent to co-operation.
Translation of his L'évolution de la propriété. First published 1892. Ethnographic and historical: holds that decrease in private holding of property will be future necessity.

On proper limits of state action relating to labor, care of poor, schools, post-office, etc. Laissez faire and individualism present in formal array the arguments by which they hope to check the tide of socialism.
Bibliography of English socialist school, p. 191-267.
Contents: How we live and how we might live: Whigs, democrats and socialists; Feudal England; Hopes of eiv- ilization; Aims of art; Useful work versus useless toil; Dawn of a new epoch.
Valuable account by a trained journalist from personal visits and observations in many communistic societies.
Third ed. with additional chapter. Statement and criticism of principles of Lassalle, Marx, Karl Marlo, the socialists of the chair, Christian socialists, Russian nihilists and Henry George.
Tho author is opponent of socialism, book is used by socialists in propaganda work and considered a fair analysis of Marx's Capital.
List of books and magazine articles, p. 283-92. If no humorous aspect of the Farm escapes him, he is quick to find and praise whatever was noble and generous in its inspiration.

Contents: Public borrowing as a financial policy; National deficit financiering; Local deficit financiering. Survey of facts as they were in 1880, with masterly statement of economic principles which should limit public indebtedness and decide its form.
Applies theory to existing conditions in United States, without touching questions of currency, banking, etc.
Discusses public expenditure, public revenues, principles of taxation, taxation on lands, business, property, consumption, ete. public credit and debts, and financial administration.
Public finance though defined as a scieuce is treated. throughout as an art. Attention is concentrated on the practical bearings of the subject.
Suggestions for students, teachers and readers, pref. p. 9-28. References at beginning of chapters.

List of authorities, pref. p. 13-15. Shows grasp of principles, thorough mastery of facts, and skill in unraveling and interpreting complex phenomena. Fairminded treatment of political parties and constant reference to original sources.
entries.noteSource: W: A. Scott in Pol. sci. q. 13: 558.

entries.note: Legislator and citizen alike may read with alternate complacency and mortification, but with uniform profit.
We might almost say, no citizen is qualified for proper discharge of his political duties without mastering the principles here expounded.
Historical sketch of prevailing tariff systems. Compact review of arguments for protection.
Analytic study from English standpoint.
Also issued under title Essays on political economy. Includes 4 parts: Sophisms of protection, 1st and 2nd ser. Spoliation and law; Capital and interest.
Leads up to doctrine that ultimate "free trade" means free access to land through operation of single tax.

entries.authorName: Laughlin, J. L., & Willis, H. P.
entries.note: Bibliography, p. 439-71. Contents: Origin and nature of the reeiprocity idea: Reciprocity with Canada; Reciprocity with Hawaii, 1876 1900; Reciprocity and the tariff controversy in the U. S. 1880-90; Reciprocity and the sugar situation; Reciprocity and the McKinley act; Operation of the McKinley act; Abandonment of reciprocity; Dingley act; Kasson treaties; Struggle for reciprocity with Cuba; Present and future of reciprocity.
Political and historical. Author protectionist, free from partizan rancor.
Accurate, noncontroversial record of facts, by a tariff reformer. For general students.

Iron and steel industries, their conditions and outlook; Midland iron and steel wages board; Cotton industry; Yorkshire woolen and worsted industries; Linen and flax industry, with special reference to Ireland; British railways as business enterprises; British shipping, and its present position; Trust movement in Great Britain.
Railroad combinations, industrial trusts, monopolies of municipal service and labor unions.

A list of books relating to trusts, p. 227-55. Eight essays by C. R. Flint, J. J. Hill, J. H. Bridge, S. C. T. Dodd and F. B. Thurber, emphasizing importance of the trust as an essential part of our industrial system, and showing its advantage as a productive agent.

1806-43. Explains importance and characteristics of fur trade, with chronologie narrative of events, biographic sketches, and a scientist's description of physical features and native tribes. Of great value for beginnings of domestic expansion and of trans-Pacific relations.
An attempt to formulate a method by which governmental control can be so exercised that the benefits of trusts may be secured and ill effects eliminated.
entries.noteSource: A. C. Pigon in Econ. j. 12: 63.

entries.note: Clear and brief explanation of consolidation of industry, with particular consideration of relations to tariff and territorial expansion.

Three very suggestive lines of thought: (1) possibility of increasing supply of nitrogen available for wheat crops by general utilization of sewage; (2) practicability of attaining the same end by electrically fixing free nitrogen of the air: (3) increasing arable lands by irrigation.

History and present status of wheat, including its place in vegetable world, use in ancient and modern times, development of wheat growing industry, flour milling and relation of tariff and transportation to wheat and flour trade.
entries.noteSource: Engin. n. v. 49, June 18 lit. sup. p. 68.

entries.note: P1. 7 of his Distribution of wealth. Full of information, moderate and impartial.

Sketches forms, objects and effects of organization, corporation law and public opinion in United States. Appendixes give specimen contracts, national and state legislation, lists of combinations, bibliography, etc.
Discussion of effects of machinery on labor, industrial depressions, women's work, wages and evolution of the trust.
Bibliographie note, p. 317-18. Brief compendium of industrial conditions as affecting combinations. By expert agent of U. S. industrial commission.
Bibliography, p. 2.
A study of trusts, particularly of the Standard oil company.
Maintains that state should guide tendency toward monopoly so that it will terminate in the passing of industry into public ownership.
Dispassionate. Extended examination of United States steel corporation of particular interest.

First published as 2 articles in the Quarterly journal of cconomics, Feb. 1902 and Feb. 1903. Pref. Study made while author was Ricardo scholar in economics at Harvard, 1900-1. Remarkably free from bias.
Advocates pensions to all persons over 65 and would meet cost by taxation on imported articles.
A fairminded statement of all the issues involved in selecting a policy for relief of the distressed.
entries.noteSource: C. E. Collet in Econ. j. 13:84.

entries.note: Outcome f 10 years actual experience as a tramp. His gift for vagabondage is like another man's gift for music. Belongs to class of books that are light reading for indolent readers, and also recognized authorities to students.
Thirteen chapters, each dealing with an institution of vital importance, which, though sometimes considered. chiefly historically, is always revealed in its present place and perspective.
Lectures on constitutions of various English speaking countries and comparison of Roman and English legal development.
He has taken the best historians of Roman law, united and vivified, extended and illustrated their conclusions in his own comprehensive way, and made obscure things luminous.

Contents: Sacred laws of the Hindus; Religion and law; Ancestor worship; Ancestor worship and inherit ance; Royal succession and the Salic law: The king in his relation to early civil justice; Theories of primitive Society; East European house communities; Decay of feudal property in France and England; Classifications of property: Classifications of legal rules; index.
List of authorities, pref. p. 47-61.
selection of works and documents on international law, p. 405-22.
Contents: pt. 1, Parliament. pt. 2. The crown. An analysis of the details of the constitution, from writs of summons to attend parliament to prorogation or dissolution of the body,
entries.noteSource: J. W. Burgess in Pol. sci. q. 1: 505 (B)

entries.note: Bibliographies.

"American preface" signed: E. L. Y. (i. e. Edward Livingston Youmans) Essays: Character of Lord Brougham; Character of Sir Robert Peel. A keen and philosophic exposition of principles. Clearly expounds difference between nominal and actnal English constitution, and the practical working relations of crown. cabinet, commons and lords.
Shows how the cabinet came into existence and how its powers developed.

Contents: v. 1, The revolution and modern France: The constitution and the chief of the state. v. 2, Parliamentary system; Political parties. From revolution. Describes clearly and from actual knowledge constitution, government, political conditions and methods. Believes centralization, not pure democracy, the ultimate destiny of France. A juster view of France does not exist in English.
A short account of its executive, legislative, judicial and municipal institutions, with an historical outline of their origin and development. Title. Elementary. Best short manual.
Principal authorities, pref. p. 9-12. Useful and lucid summary of principal points in evolution of federal system in Canada. French régime passed over briefly.

Contents: v. 1, The national government: The state governments. v. 2, The party system; Publie opinion; Illustrations and reflections; Social institutions. Abridged ed. $1.75 n Of rare philosophic power and insight, easily first among descriptions and criticisms of American political and social institutions. Based on extensive personal knowledge of U.S. as well as thorough study of its history.

Contents: v. 1, Sovereignty and liberty. v. 2, Government. Comparison of constitutional systems of United States. Great Britain, France and Germany, from point of view of an abstruse theoretic discussion of the nature of goy- ernment, state and nation. Author's personal views strongly emphasized.
Best brief manual. Systematic, simple and clear; exposition admirable.
History and development outlined. Defects and inconsistencies of existing machinery of government pointed out and possible remedies suggested.
Best introductory book on English constitution. Contains thoughtful analysis of U. S. constitution.

Written at the very birth of the Union by those who watched its cradle, and recording, incidentally, and therefore all the more faithfully, the impressions and anticipations of the friends and enemies of the infant constitution.
Attractively written elementary account, descriptive and historical.
Aims to explain causes rather than narrate events, so that a reader may understand our actual system of gov ernment.
Shows to what extent modern civilization has adopted ancient political ideas. Valuabie as introduction to study of ancient history.
Little and good. Covers in some 150 pages the whole course of the constitution. The argument clear and direct, the English simple and manly.
A discussion of causes. Based on original sources; choice of facts and arguments made with great skill and judgment.
Its value depends not so much on amount of ascertained truth as on the new angle at which it presents every fact and institution of the ancient world.
entries.noteSource: H. A. L. Fisher in Eng. hist. r. 5: 3 (B)

entries.note: Still valuable, though in light of later research much of the information needs correction. Written with insight, sound judgment and impartiality, but has whig bias.
Select bibliography of American government. Pref. p. 13-34. An attempt to describe the government as one might undertake to describe a great railroad.
No other historian has followed out the main lines of our historical development with so keen a logic or so independent a spirit.
entries.noteSource: H. Adams and H. C. Lodge in No. Amer. 123: 328.

entries.note: Shows importance of law and government, and explains U. S. local and national systems. Emphasizes personal responsibility.

entries.authorName: James, J. A., & Sanford, A. H.
entries.note: Reference books, p. 375-78. Textbook for secondary schools. Chapters supplemented by questions and references.

Studies relations between development of parties and mechanism of government, sketching recent history of France, Italy, Germany, Austro-Hungary and Switzerland. Appendix contains constitutions in original languages.

Purpose to show ever changing character of American constitution by comparing and contrasting it with history and latest development of English constitution. One of best accounts of organization and operation of British parliamentary government.

History of parties, the press and liberty of opinion, personal liberty, religious liberty, loeal as well as eentral government, Ireland before the Union, government of British colonies and dependencies and the progress of general legislation.
Treats subject by topics. Marginal references to standard works. Brief synopses of some important cases in English constitutional law appended. Eminently usable and accurate.
Bibliography, p. 349-56.
Vol. 1, 6th ed. 1897; v. 2, 4th ed. 1896; v. 3, 5th ed. 1896. In depth and thoroughness of research, keenness of insight, soundness of judgment, unsurpassed.
One of the few treatises on the philosophy of politics which has risen to the rank of a classic.
Literature. p. 341-60. Exhaustive exposition of the whole framework and administration of Swiss government.
The best survey, at once concise and comprehensive, of English law that has ever appeared.

Shows how rules of law governing ordinary business transactions have been developed, defines common legal terms, teaches proper forms and uses of negotiable paper, gives useful information concerning eonveyance of land, ete.
Ingenious; temperate; rich in thought, argument and brilliant intuitions.
Complete institutes of Roman law, aside from law of actions. Style characterized by peculiar precision and often enlightened by colloquial vivacity and even humor.

Seeks to give concise comparative view of administrative as distinguished from constitutional law. Based on first hand study but written for students rather than mature scholars. Point of view not seldom European.
Lays much stress on extra-legal institutions and gives interestingly the history and philosophy of such spontaneous political growths as the party, the spoils system and the boss.
Reviews, in extended summary form, the leading features of all the more important ancient and modern systems of government.
What the government elassified service now is, qualifications required in eandidates, and many examples of recent papers. Dissipates misleading impressions of these examinations.
Papers by experts on waterworks, electric and gas lighting, the telephone, and street railways. Favors municipal ownership.

Bibliography, p. 8-9. Aims to point out tendencies in the past and present and to describe and illustrate the progress in the spirit of municipal reform. Appendix gives some suggestive programs and platforms for municipal leagues.
Past trend and present status clearly shown.
For municipal officers without engineering training.
study of relations of city and state from legal point of view, with special reference to question of home rule for American cities.
Argues forcibly that local affairs should be controlled by city council rather than mayor, matters of general concern by a permanent state board of supervision.

Presents essential framework and functioning of French, German and Austrian cities, with special studies of the larger and more progressive cities. Full of suggestions for American students and reformers.
Does for Glasgow, Manchester, Birmingham and London what the preceding volume does for continental Europe.
Bibliographie note, p. 476-78. Study of facts, present tendencies and ultimate results of modern drift of population to cities the world over. Accurate.

Contents: Municipal sociology; Transportation: Public works; Sanitation; Public schools; Public libraries; Pub- lie buildings: Parks and boulevards; Public recreation; Public control, ownership, and operation.
Underguise of a tour to Washington by a party of boys and girls, author describes actual workings of national government in its various departments. Photographic illustrations.
Explains government, voting, taxes, etc. and shows that children should be good citizens.
Constitution and practical workings of Congress, the presidency, executive departments, judiciary, Smithsonian institution, civil service and other commissions.

Contents: The presidency, by T. Roosevelt; Life of a senator, by H: C. Lodge; Life of a congressman, by T: B. Reed: United States supreme court, by D: J. Brewer: How Jack lives, by J: D. Long: Naval war college, by J: D. Long: How our soldiers are fed, by W. C. Sanger; How the army is clothed, by M. F. Ludington; Good manners and diplomacy, by W: R. Day: How foreign. treaties are made, by H: C. Lodge: Uncle Sam's law business, by J. R. Richards; American post office, by W. L. Wilson. For older boys and girls.
Describes training of army officers; studies, drill, discipline and amusements.
Describes development of American charities to present organization and special training.
Appendix containing suggestions, references, etc., p. 349-94. Compendious, suggestive and enlightening. Alto gether the best book of its kind either for general reading or for classroom work.
Brief bibliography, pref. p. 9-10. Indispensable for the practical worker among the poor.
A perfect little manual.

Essays on social settlements, principles and dangers of charity administration, philanthropy and morality, etc. by Jane Addams, R. A. Woods, Father Huntington, F. H: Giddings and Beraard Bosanquet. Practical and stimulating.
Bibliographic index, p. 421-30. Review of current methods of Amer. charities, with informed and sensible criticism. Admirable for practical worker.
From no other work of like compass can so much useful information on this subject be obtained. Bibliographies.
Record of observations and meditations of a man of experience. Conclusious summarized in a working program at end.
Illustration of the value of personal service and ringing indictment of society for its attitude toward the ex-convict.
A wonderful book. Shows by personal investigation of a single pauper tribe, traced back 150 years, the relations of heredity and crime.
Review of results reached by students of criminal anthropology in Italy, France, Germany, England and the U. S. with criticism.
Argues that only hope of diminishing habitual eriminal population is to lessen number of recruits, most of whom are to be found between the ages of 16 and 21.

Written round the thesis that in dealing with juvenile crime the only method which holds out any reasonable prospect of success is educational, not punitive. By far the best and most suggestive work [1897] on juvenile crime in our language.
One of the best known and most popular works on crime. Author secretary of the Howard association, London, and his counsels deserve attention.
Authorities, pref. p. 8. Deserves attention of students and professional men. In no other one book can one find the essential questions as well treated for the American public.

Contents: Meaning of education; What knowledge is of most worth? Is there a new education? Democracy and education; The American college and the American university; Function of the secondary school; Reform of see- ondary education in the United States.
Brief bibliography, p. 245-46.
Bibliography, p. 257-68.

Based on belief that education consists, not alone in developing the intellect, but in forming, guiding or repressing the feelings and impulses, and that doctrine of interest applied to education will lead to this larger and deeper culture.
Contents: The school and social progress; School and the life of the child; Waste in education; Three years of the University elementary school.
Social rather than scholastic point of view. For parents and teachers.

Teachers' tenure of office; Education of ministers: Can school programs be shortened and enriched? Electives in college admission requirements, etc. Addresses 1869-1897. A plea for unification of educational forces from lowest to highest and for adaptation of teaching to the individual.

entries.authorName: Felkin, H: M., & Felkin, Mrs Emmie.
entries.note: Answers question: Who is Herbart and what did he and bis followers teach? better than any account of the Herbartian method hitherto published in English.
Includes, among others, critical studies of Socrates, Ascham, Thring, Joseph Lancaster and Pestalozzi.

Contents: Point of view: The social purpose; Source of power; Organic education: Cause and effect; Childhood; Youth; Holidays; At the university; The experimental life; The agents of the social purpose. Its main value lies in its sincere and inspiring idealism.
Contrasts points of difference in educational systems of Germany, France, England and the U. S.

Contents: Joseph Priestley; On the educational value of the natural history sciences; Emancipation, black and white; A liberal education, and where to find it; Scientific education; Science and culture; On science and art in relation to education; Universities, actual and ideal; Address on university education; On the study of biology; On elementary instruction in physiology; On medical education; The state and medical profession; Connection of the biological sciences with medicine; School boards, what they can do and what they may do; Technical education; Address on behalf of the National association for the promotion of technical education.

Enough psychology to answer the present purpose, presented in beautifully clear and simple English and well illustrated by examples drawn from common observation. One of its charms is its uniform good sense.
Of all Locke's works perhaps the most universally approved; in truth a golden treatise, the very incarnation of good sense and right feeling.
Simple presentation of aim of education, relative value of studies, doctrine of interest, culture epochs, theory of arranging studies and apperception from Herbartian point of view.

Contents: Cloistral schools; The Palatine school; Medieval university life; University colleges, origin and methods: The primary school in the middle ages; Simultaneous method in teaching; Beginnings of the normal school; M. Gabriel Compayré as an historian of pedagogy.
Formerly National teachers' association.
Relates both physiology and psychology to growth of character, development of mental power, education of imagination, control of emotions, training of the rea- son and guidance of will.
Marked by clear thinking, deep sympathy, reverent faith in God and human nature, high ideals and practical ideas as to working them out.
Not only one of the most readable but also one of the most important books in the English language.
Condensed statement of aims and systems of education. Largely devoted to education in France.
Specially useful bibliographies accompany each subject. of use to librarians, students of educational history, and above all to teachers planning or developing such a course.
Prominence given to different stages in growth of Greek political, ethical and religious consciousness.
Bibliography, p. 277-82. Attempts to correlate each system of education with the age which formulated it and to point out the historical and philosophic evolution.
Bibliography, p. 355-59. Aims to single out those events which illustrate most clearly the genesis and evolution of existing systems and method.

Traces development of educational ideals and methods by a series of keen illuminating essays on 14 great leaders from renaissance to present day. Most valuable history of education in our mother tongne [1897]
. Examines and compares systems developed in Germany, France and U. S. for education of industrial classes and points out need of organization in England.

Treats of location, construction, ventilation, heating, lighting, sanitary care, furniture, and of details of form, finish and decoration. Suggestive chapter on beauty in school work. List of suitable pictures and casts.
Bibliography, p. 276-78.

Delivered at Cambridge univ. 1880. As a popular exposition of the art of teaching it is unsurpassed [1903] Impressive by its wide outlook, sound common sense, largemindedness and expository power. Expressed in simple, lucid, harmonious English.
Third ed. of his Manual training.
Aims to make this art an effective tool in hands of pupils by such readjustment of relations between pupil and teacher as shall make the pupil the center of the teaching system.
Thorough, concrete, simple, clear.
entries.noteSource: C. C. Van Liew in Educ. r. 15:188.

entries.note: Valuable book on methods for elementary subjects,
Careful analysis of the psychologie bases of good thinking. Clearly written, richly and pointedly illustrated. Helpful and stimulating to teachers.

Bibliography, p. 253-55. On building, grounds, heating, ventilation, baths, furniture, postures and exercises, eyesight, hearing, handwriting, contagious diseases, etc. A valuable contribution to the subject, the outcome of intelligent study and large experience.
entries.noteSource: A. P. Marble in Educ. r. 22-412-15.

entries.note: He has liited the whole business of school condnet to a high moral elevation. The teacher is little to be envied who can read these pages without feeling the sacredness of his calling and appreciating his responsibility.
entries.noteSource: W: H. Maxwell in Educ. r. (B)

entries.note: Printed also in Educ. r. March, 1895.

By a physician in a child's hospital. Holds that environment transcends heredity in influence and emphasizes importance of scientide preparation for care of children. Criticises present primary school methods.
Distinctly a physiologic study of the growth of the child, from early years through adolescence, giving special attention to nerve signs of all kinds. Simply written and free from technicalities.
To those who have sat bewildered by words intended to explain the Mother-play these simple, direct teachings will be a revelation.

Discusses practically the foundations of Froebel's philosophy and shows clearly significance of the kindergarten and its claims for the important place of cornerstone of education. For mothers as well as teachers.
Standard work, published in 1826, containing a full exposition of Froebel's philosophy. It measures every intellectual activity by its influence on character.
Verse translations by various writers. Original music replaced by new or newly selected melodies.
Talks by an experienced kindergartner; suggestive and helpful to mothers and teachers,
Main object to show that Froebel's ideas and methods are significant for whole sehemie of education from kindergarten to university.
Series of morning talks and stories for a full year A pure child's storybook with scientific truth and deep purpose.
The interpretation of the spiritual side of the kindergarten. Not a technical book.

entries.authorName: Wiggin, Mrs K.. D. (Smith), & Smith, N. A.
entries.note: Contents: v.1, Froebel's gifts; v. 2, Froebel's occupations; v. 3, Kindergarten principles and practice. An untechnical setting forth of the modern American adaptation of Froebel's philosophy. Displays much wit, wisdom and philosophy.
Bibliography, p. 481-518.

Contents: The great question; Tact: On money matters; Recreation; Health; National education; Self-education: On libraries; On reading: Patriotism; Citizenship; Social life; Industry: Faith; Hope; Charity: Character: On peace. and happiness; Religion. It suggests thoughts; it answers questions without troubling us to ask them: reasons and does not dogmatize; it is cheerful, humorous, charitable and conscientious.

entries.authorName: Brookings, W. D., & Ringwalt, R. C. l.
entries.note: Bibliography of debating, pref. p. 41-47. With each subject, references to articles and leading points pro and con are given.
Familiar chapters on how to talk, write, go in society, and various other things sometimes dreaded by young people because they are not sure just "how."

Practical and suggestive talks on education, power of time, influence of money, women and marriage, society and solitude, surroundings, ete. from the point of view of an accomplished art critic and author.

Contents: History: Biography; Politics; Political economy: Education: Literature; Art; Science; Philosophy: Ethics: Religion: Miscellaneous; Questions with references; Questions without references; Cyclopedias and periodicals referred to, with abbreviated forms.
Contents: Purpose; Friends and companions; Manners; Thrift: Self-reliance and courage; Health: Reading: Amusements; Purity: Faith.
On health, education, self-support, charity, hospi tality, emotional women, ete. The cogency of the reasoning is no less remarkable than its persuasiveness.
Inspiriting, practical suggestions for making the most of life. Full of pithy extracts and anecdotes.
Discusses discipline, curriculums, games, gymnas ties, the monitorial system, the training of teachers.. methods of teaching modern languages, etc. Emphasizes study of the classies.
Combines with a historie review and vigorous arguments many valuable statements of facts in England, France, Germany and other countries.
Discusses problems of woman's college life, her preparatory work, studies, environment, health and her duties to and influence on the community.
Holds that public schools should train moral perceptions and teach filial, fraternal and civic duties. Discusses practicable, non-sectarian methods.
Historical development and analysis.
Bibliography, p. 307-9. Four parts: origin, organization, course of study and methods of teaching, general spirit and influence. Abelard occupies but a small part of the volume.
Addresses before educational institutions setting forth the ideal of a university and its relation to modern life. Optimistic.

These diseourses powerfully enforce the true purpose of liberal education, that it is a pursuit of knowledge for the sake of knowledge and not for the value of any of its fruits or applications, however important.
Local guide-book, university history and educational essay all in one.
entries.noteSource: N: M. Butler in Educ. r., 7: 500 (B)

entries.note: Sums up results of public education, its benefits and shortcomings. Suggests definite constructive measures for improvement. Urgesmuch greater expenditures.
List of books, pref p. 23-26. Treats economic principles as illustrated in commercial life.
In the main discourages state interference.
